scenarios.title: The Cousin Nobody Remembers
scenarios.text: Someone from your hometown with your last name, a folder of drawings and a business idea is waiting by your car after practice. He says you met at a wedding when you were nine.

choices.label: Hear the pitch, then check it
choices.result: You listen, take the paperwork and have your agent look at it. The idea is real; the numbers aren't. You say no with reasons.

choices.label: Buy him lunch, not the idea
choices.result: You buy him lunch and talk about family for an hour. You don't invest, and he leaves happier than he came.

choices.label: Say no before he finishes
choices.result: No, before he's finished his first sentence, and you get in your car. It's quick and a little cold, and {parent} hears about it from three relatives by Sunday.

scenarios.title: The Equipment Upgrade
scenarios.text: A sales rep corners you after practice with expensive training equipment: a sensor suit, a kicking machine, and an app that charts every kick you've ever taken. He has a tablet and a very good smile.

choices.label: Buy the full setup
choices.result: All of it, delivered Thursday. The data is incredible, your living room is full of machines, and the bill is the kind you read twice.

choices.label: Use what the club has
choices.result: The club's staff charts you with what they already have. It's less fancy and nearly as good, and the trainer likes being asked.

choices.label: Keep it simple
choices.result: Your leg doesn't need an app, you decide. The rep leaves his card, your weeks stay simple, and you never think about sensor suits again.

scenarios.title: The Wind Tunnel
scenarios.text: The stadium's wind swirls in a way no film can show: in from the left at the bottom, out to the right at the top. The veterans just laugh when you ask about it.

choices.label: Kick in it every day
choices.result: Every day after practice, you kick into the swirl until you can feel it before it moves the ball. Your leg is sore, and the swirl stops surprising you.

choices.label: Ask the grounds crew
choices.result: The grounds crew have watched that wind for twenty years. They show you exactly which flags to watch, and one of them draws you a map on a napkin.

choices.label: Listen at lunch instead
choices.result: Instead of asking, you listen at lunch. Three veterans tell you everything about the wind, one story at a time, over a week.

scenarios.title: The Scout Team
scenarios.text: You spend practice kicking for the scout team, against the starters, and nobody important watches. The coaches are at the other end of the field.

choices.label: Treat it like the real thing
choices.result: Every scout-team rep, like it's the real thing. Nobody watches, and you get better anyway, and the scout-team players start cheering your makes.

choices.label: Get to know the scout team
choices.result: Every name on the scout team, learned by Friday. They become your favorite people in the building, and they save you a seat on the bus.

choices.label: Save your leg
choices.result: Easy reps, and your leg stays fresh. It's sensible, and you notice by Thursday that you don't feel like part of anything.

scenarios.title: The Weight Room Pecking Order
scenarios.text: The weight room has a pecking order, and rookies lift last, after the linemen are done with every rack. By the time you get a bench, it's lunch.

choices.label: Lift at dawn
choices.result: Six in the morning, before the linemen arrive. It's lonely and very effective, and the strength coach starts unlocking the door for you.

choices.label: Spot a lineman
choices.result: An offer to spot a veteran lineman, and he accepts with suspicion. By the end of the week, he's saving you a rack and calling you 'kicker' fondly.

choices.label: Take what's left
choices.result: Whatever's free, without making a thing of it. Nobody notices you, which is fine for now, and you finish your lifts on the stretching mats.

scenarios.title: The Equipment Manager
scenarios.text: The equipment manager can make your life easy or miserable: cleats, balls, the locker by the heater or the one by the door. You've been here a week and haven't said hello.

choices.label: Bring coffee
choices.result: Coffee for the equipment staff on Monday, and you learn every name. Your cleats are perfect all season, and you end up in the locker by the heater.

choices.label: Ask how the balls are prepared
choices.result: How are game balls prepared? He tells you all of it, for an hour, with visible joy. You learn more about kicking than you expected.

choices.label: Keep it professional
choices.result: Hello, thank you and nothing more. It's fine, nothing special happens, and your locker stays the one by the door.

scenarios.title: The First Fine
scenarios.text: A fine slip in your locker after the first team flight: a dress-code violation you didn't know existed. Your socks, apparently, were the wrong color, and the veterans have already framed a photo of them.

choices.label: Laugh and pay it
choices.result: Paid in cash, with a grin, and you wear the loudest socks you own to the next team meal. The room loves it, and the fine committee adds a new rule in your honor.

choices.label: Read the whole rulebook
choices.result: The full team rulebook, forty pages, read in bed that night. You find two more rules you've been breaking and fix both before anyone notices.

choices.label: Pay it and go kick
choices.result: Paid, with some grumbling, and the irritation goes straight into an extra session at the net. Your leg feels better than your pride by dinner.

scenarios.title: The Meal Money
scenarios.text: The per diem envelope on the first road trip is thicker than any scholarship check you ever got in college. The veterans are already planning where theirs is going tonight.

choices.label: Put it in the bank
choices.result: The whole envelope goes in the bank, and you eat the team meals. By December the road trips have quietly paid for your offseason trainer.

choices.label: Take the rookies out
choices.result: The rookie class eats like kings for one night on your envelope. It's gone by dessert, and four rookies will remember it for years.

choices.label: Treat yourself, a little
choices.result: A good dinner alone, a good book from the airport and a long nap. It feels like being a grown-up, and you send {parent} a photo of the dessert.

scenarios.title: Rookie Year Taxes
scenarios.text: Your first tax bill as a pro arrives in a thick envelope: a number nobody prepared you for, due in a month, with forms from every state you played a road game in.

choices.label: Hire an athletes' accountant
choices.result: An accountant who only works with athletes takes the whole envelope off your hands. It's done in two weeks, correctly, and you learn what a 'jock tax' is.

choices.label: Ask a veteran at lunch
choices.result: One veteran at lunch gives you his accountant's number and a story about his first year that makes you laugh until your stomach hurts.

choices.label: Do it yourself
choices.result: A long weekend with spreadsheets and coffee. It's stressful, probably right, and you feel strangely proud when you click the last button.

scenarios.title: Free Cleats
scenarios.text: A shoe company offers you free cleats and a small contract, if you wear them on camera. The cleats are bright orange, and your old pair has been with you since college.

choices.label: Sign and lace up
choices.result: Signed, and the orange cleats arrive the next day. They're fine, the check pays for your offseason training, and the veterans call you 'traffic cone'.

choices.label: Test them for a week
choices.result: A week of testing before you sign anything. They're good, so you sign, with a clause that lets you wear your old pair if they ever hurt.

choices.label: Keep your old cleats
choices.result: Your old cleats stay. Your feet are happy and your account is the same, and the equipment manager pats them like an old dog.

scenarios.title: The Kicking Ball Room
scenarios.text: The equipment staff prepares the game balls in a back room that smells like leather and brushes, and you have opinions about how the balls feel. Nobody has asked for them yet.

choices.label: Learn how it's done
choices.result: An afternoon in the ball room with the staff, watching every step. Your opinions get much better informed, and much quieter.

choices.label: Thank the staff every day
choices.result: A thank-you after every practice, every day. By October they start showing you the game balls on Friday, which nobody else gets.

choices.label: Kick every practice ball
choices.result: Every practice ball, kicked, until you can feel the difference between them in your sleep. Your leg aches, and the balls stop surprising you.

scenarios.title: The Trainer's Table
scenarios.text: The athletic trainer presses a thumb into your hip and says your hip flexor is tight. You think it's nothing. The trainer is still pressing, and looking at you over their glasses.

choices.label: Do the stretches
choices.result: Every stretch, every day, exactly as written. The tightness is gone in a week, and the trainer says 'told you' with great satisfaction.

choices.label: Kick on it anyway
choices.result: Kicking through it works: the hip holds. It nags all month, like a stone in your shoe, and you start every practice a little worried.

choices.label: Take a day off kicking
choices.result: A full day off kicking, which feels like a crime. It helps more than you'd like to admit, and you come back loose.

scenarios.title: Your First Locker
scenarios.text: Your name is on a strip of tape above a locker between two veterans who haven't introduced themselves. One is eating a sandwich. The other is staring at you like you're a rumor.

choices.label: Introduce yourself to both
choices.result: A handshake from one, a grunt from the other. By October, the grunt is your favorite person in the building and steals your snacks.

choices.label: Let your work introduce you
choices.result: Head down, work loud. It takes a month, and when the welcome comes it's real: the grunting veteran saves you a seat on the plane.

choices.label: Make the locker yours
choices.result: A photo of your family and a paper calendar go up first. It makes the place feel like yours, and {parent} asks for a picture of it.
